subtype: Long scarcity leaves little room for planning [Observer]
passage: Farida had been a caseworker at the community centre for six years, and she had learned to watch hands. Nandini's hands shook as she held the savings workshop form. She had been sleeping on a bus-stand bench for a month since the landlord changed the locks, and cleaning offices at night. "I'll fill it later," she said, and folded it into a tiny square. A colleague muttered that some people just don't try. Farida thought: when every hour is about tonight's food and a safe corner, there is no room left for next year. That's scarcity, not a lack of effort. She found Nandini a bed at the working women's hostel and meal tokens for two weeks. On the fourteenth day, Nandini asked her about the tailoring course.

qa.q: Where had Nandini been sleeping for a month?
qa.a: On a bus-stand bench, since the landlord changed the locks.

qa.q: What does Nandini folding the form into a tiny square suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt overwhelmed and could not face planning ahead while she was worried about food and a safe place to sleep.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida made the difference, and why?
qa.a: Farida arranged a hostel bed and meal tokens first instead of pushing the form, and once those basics were steady, Nandini had room in her mind to ask about the course.

qa.q: How does the colleague see Nandini, and what does that miss?
qa.a: The colleague sees someone who doesn't try, which misses that she was exhausted and focused on surviving each night.

grounding: A caseworker sees that a woman without safe shelter or regular food cannot plan ahead, and that stable basics free her to think about the future.

passage:
Subject: Harun and the training sign-up
Hi Uday,
You asked why I didn't issue Harun a warning for missing the forklift training sign-up again. I asked him about it on Friday. He told me he's been sleeping on a cousin's floor since his flat flooded in the monsoon, working our day shift and a night job, and often skipping lunch to save. He said the sign-up just slips out of his head. I believe him. When someone is running on so little, next month's course can't compete with tonight's bed. I've moved him to steady shifts, pointed him to the housing help desk, and told him lunch in the canteen is covered this month. I'll book the training for him in six weeks, once things settle. Can we keep this out of his file?
Pallavi

qa.q: Why has Harun been sleeping on a cousin's floor?
qa.a: His flat flooded in the monsoon.

qa.q: Why did Pallavi believe Harun's explanation?
qa.a: Pallavi felt sympathy for Harun, seeing that with two jobs, little sleep and skipped lunches, his forgetting came from strain rather than carelessness.

qa.q: What was the key choice Pallavi made instead of a warning?
qa.a: Pallavi steadied his shifts, pointed him to housing help and covered his lunch, then planned the training for later, so the basics come first.

qa.q: How might Uday view Harun differently after this email?
qa.a: Uday may stop seeing Harun as unreliable and instead see someone under heavy pressure who needs support, not a mark in his file.

grounding: A manager notices that a worker short of sleep, food and safe housing cannot keep up with planning tasks, and gives support instead of blame.

subtype: Long scarcity leaves little room for planning [Observer]
passage: You want to know about Yogesh? Okay. I'm Swati, and he's been my closest friend since college. Two years ago his father fell ill, the savings went, and Yogesh lost his job the same month. He moved into a room with a leaking roof, ate one meal a day, and slept badly because of the dripping. Everyone asked me, 'Why isn't he applying anywhere? Is he lazy?' But when I visited, I saw him staring at a job site for an hour without typing. He couldn't think past dinner. My parents offered him our spare room. After a month of three meals and dry nights, he was making a list of companies, and then a timetable. Same person. He just finally had some space in his head.

qa.q: What did Yogesh eat each day while in the room with the leaking roof?
qa.a: He ate one meal a day.

qa.q: What did Swati think when seeing Yogesh stare at the job site without typing?
qa.a: Swati realised he wasn't lazy; he was so worn down by hunger and bad sleep that he couldn't think past dinner.

qa.q: What choice changed things for Yogesh?
qa.a: Accepting the spare room from Swati's parents gave him steady meals and dry nights, and with those basics he began planning his job search.

qa.q: Why might the people who called Yogesh lazy have seen him differently if they had visited like Swati?
qa.a: They would have seen the leaking roof and the single meal, and understood that his stuck state came from scarcity, not a lack of will.

grounding: A friend tells how long hunger and poor shelter left a young man unable to plan, and how stable basics freed his mind.

passage:
I'm Tarun. I run the tea stall outside the metro station in Hyderabad, and for most of last year, Anand was a regular.
He was a delivery rider, about twenty-four, always on his phone for orders. I found out slowly that he slept in a shared room with eight men and ate once a day, mostly my bun and chai. When the youth centre next door put up a poster for a free computer course, the other riders teased him: "Too lazy to fill a form?" He just shrugged and said, "Next month." Next month never came.
Then in spring a social worker from the centre helped him get a hostel bed and a meal card. Within weeks he looked different, less grey. One morning he borrowed my pen and filled that form, right here on my counter.
He wasn't lazy. He was just too tired and hungry to think past today.

qa.q: Where did Anand fill in the form?
qa.a: Right here on my counter, at Tarun's tea stall.

qa.q: What does Anand's 'Next month' suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: It suggests he had no room to think ahead; being hungry and exhausted every day kept all his attention on getting through today.

qa.q: What turning point allowed Anand to plan ahead, and why?
qa.a: Getting a hostel bed and a meal card through the social worker gave him steady basics, which freed his mind to fill the form.

qa.q: How did the other riders see Anand, and why might they have been wrong?
qa.a: They saw him as lazy, but Tarun noticed that he slept in a crowded room and ate once a day, which left no energy for planning.

grounding: It shows, through a tea-seller's eyes, a young man short of food, sleep and shelter who cannot plan until stable basics free his mind, showing scarcity rather than laziness.

subtype: Long scarcity leaves little room for planning [Observer]
passage:
Week one. Pooja ran the evening sewing course at the women's centre in Nagpur. Vasudha, twenty-five, came late and left early. She was living with her two children in a corner of a relative's room, sleeping little, eating whatever was left. When Pooja asked about the stall she wanted one day, Vasudha said, "I can't think about one day, Didi. I can only think about tonight."
Week four. The centre found Vasudha and her children a room in a shelter home with regular meals. She came on time for the first time. She fell asleep once over the machine, and Pooja let her be.
Week nine. Vasudha arrived with a small notebook. Inside, in careful writing, was a list: blouse orders, the cost of thread, the name of a market. "I started planning," she said, almost shy. Pooja realised it had never been about effort.

qa.q: What did the centre find for Vasudha and her children?
qa.a: A room in a shelter home with regular meals.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she said she could only think about tonight?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and stuck in the present, because finding food and a place to sleep each day left no room in her mind for the future.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Vasudha, and what did it make possible?
qa.a: Getting a stable room and regular meals was the turning point; with basics steady, she could come on time and start a written plan for her stall.

qa.q: How did Pooja's view of Vasudha change over the weeks?
qa.a: Pooja came to see that Vasudha's lateness and lack of plans came from scarcity, not a lack of effort.

grounding: It shows over several weeks how a woman short of shelter, food and sleep cannot plan until stable basics free her mind, as observed by her teacher.
